the primary parasitaemias of P. inui in Rhesus monkeys occurred 31 and 31 days after inoculation with 8.6 x 10(3) and 5.93 X 10(6), respectively, of sporozoites dissected from the infected salivary glands.

the development of the sporozoites of P. inui in Rhesus monkeys and the effect of chloroguanidine on the development.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
chloroguanide, a 5-nitroimidazole, is effective in the prophylaxis of Plasmodial infection in the Rhesus monkey, but not in the prevention of infection in man.
chloroguanide can induce retarded exoerytrocytic schizont formation in the liver of Rhesus monkeys infected with P. inui.
chloroguanide can be used as a chemoprophylactic drug against sporozoite-induced infection of malaria.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the sporozoites of P. inui in Macaques can be induced to form the exoerythroctytic schizonts and the primary parasitaemias can be delayed for 24 d by the moderate doses of chloroquine.
the chloroguanide is a potent drug for prophylaxis and treatment of malaria.

the chloroguanide was not able to suppress the primary parasitaemic attack in monkeys infected with a large number sporozoites, but the retarded schizonts could be found in the liver of the infected animals.
The main takeaway from our work is that
chloroguanide may be used to delay primary parasitaemia of P. inui in Rhesus monkeys.
the chloroguanide is a good candidate for the treatment of malaria in humans.
the chloroguanide treatment is a good model for the induction of retarded exo-erythrocytic stages of P. inui in Rhesus monkey.
